claim: Many commercial antibodies do not recognize their intended targets.
source: It is commonly understood that many commercial antibodies do not recognize their intended targets, but information on the scope of the problem remains largely anecdotal, and as such, feasibility of the goal of at least one potent and specific antibody targeting each protein in a proteome cannot be assessed.
evidence: This is stated as commonly understood knowledge in the field, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: 614 commercial antibodies for 65 neuroscience-related proteins were assessed using standardized characterization approaches.
source: Focusing on antibodies for human proteins, we have scaled a standardized characterization approach using parental and knockout cell lines (Laflamme et al., 2019) to assess the performance of 614 commercial antibodies for 65 neuroscience-related proteins.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental work performed, with specific numbers of antibodies and proteins tested.

claim: More than 50% of all antibodies failed in one or more applications.
source: Side-by-side comparisons of all antibodies against each target, obtained from multiple commercial partners, have demonstrated that: (i) more than 50% of all antibodies failed in one or more applications
evidence: This is a direct result from the experimental testing of 614 antibodies across multiple applications.

claim: Approximately 50-75% of the protein set was covered by at least one high-performing antibody, depending on application.
source: yet, ~50–75% of the protein set was covered by at least one high-performing antibody, depending on application, suggesting that coverage of human proteins by commercial antibodies is significant
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data showing coverage rates across different applications.

claim: Recombinant antibodies performed better than monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies.
source: recombinant antibodies performed better than monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the experimental testing of different antibody types.

claim: Hundreds of underperforming antibodies identified in this study were found to have been used in a large number of published articles.
source: The hundreds of underperforming antibodies identified in this study were found to have been used in a large number of published articles, which should raise alarm.
evidence: This is based on bibliometric analysis using CiteAb to track usage of tested antibodies in the literature.

claim: More than half of the underperforming commercial antibodies were reassessed by the manufacturers, and many had alterations to their recommended usage or were removed from the market.
source: Encouragingly, more than half of the underperforming commercial antibodies were reassessed by the manufacturers, and many had alterations to their recommended usage or were removed from the market.
evidence: This is based on feedback from participating antibody manufacturers about actions taken in response to the characterization data.

claim: There are approximately 1.6 million commercially available antibodies targeting approximately 96% of human proteins.
source: The research enterprise spends significantly on the ~1.6 M commercially available antibodies targeting ~96% of human proteins (Bandrowski et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bandrowski et al., 2023.

claim: $0.375 to $1.75 billion is wasted yearly on non-specific antibodies.
source: Unfortunately, a significant percentage of these antibodies do not recognize the intended protein or recognize the protein but also recognize non-intended targets, with estimates that $0.375 to $1.75 billion is wasted yearly on non-specific antibodies (Baker, 2015; Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Voskuil et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baker, 2015; Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Voskuil et al., 2020.

claim: The use of poor-quality antibodies is a major factor in the scientific reproducibility crisis.
source: Perhaps worse, the use of poor-quality antibodies is a major factor in the scientific reproducibility crisis (Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Voskuil et al., 2020; Baker, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Voskuil et al., 2020; Baker, 2020.

claim: The optimal antibody testing methodology uses an appropriately selected wild type cell and an isogenic CRISPR knockout version of the same cell.
source: The optimal antibody testing methodology is largely settled; using an appropriately selected wild type cell and an isogenic CRISPR knockout (KO) version of the same cell as the basis for testing, yields rigorous and broadly applicable results (this study, as well as Laflamme et al., 2019; Ellis et al., 2023; Davies et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies including the current study, Laflamme et al., 2019; Ellis et al., 2023; Davies et al., 2013.

claim: The cost of KO-based validation is estimated at $25,000.
source: However, the cost of antibody characterization using engineered KO cells is higher than that of other methods, mainly because of the cost of custom edited cells. Commercial antibody suppliers support a large and diverse catalogue of products, with most antibody products generating <$5000 in total sales, far less than the costs of KO-based validation, estimated at $25,000.
evidence: This is an estimate provided by the authors based on their experience with the validation process.

claim: The partnership includes 10 companies representing approximately 27% of antibody manufacturing worldwide.
source: We created a partnership of academics, funders, and commercial antibody manufacturers, including 10 companies representing approximately 27% of antibody manufacturing worldwide.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the composition of the partnership formed for this study.

claim: Approximately two thirds of the protein set was covered by at least one high-performing antibody.
source: We have tested 614 commercially available antibodies targeting 65 proteins, and found that approximately two thirds of this protein set was covered by at least one high-performing antibody, and half was covered by at least one high-performing renewable antibody, suggesting that coverage of human proteins by high-performing antibodies is significant.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental testing of antibodies.

claim: Half of the protein set was covered by at least one high-performing renewable antibody.
source: We have tested 614 commercially available antibodies targeting 65 proteins, and found that approximately two thirds of this protein set was covered by at least one high-performing antibody, and half was covered by at least one high-performing renewable antibody, suggesting that coverage of human proteins by high-performing antibodies is significant.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental testing of antibodies.

claim: The 65 target proteins comprise 32 Alzheimer's disease-related proteins, 22 ALS-related proteins, 5 Parkinson's disease-linked proteins, and 6 industry-nominated proteins.
source: The list is comprises 32 Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related proteins that were community-nominated through an NIH-funded project on dark AD genes (https://agora.adknowledgeportal.org/), 22 proteins nominated within the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) Reproducible Antibody Platform project, 5 Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked proteins nominated by the Michael J. Fox Foundation, and 6 proteins nominated by industry (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the composition of the protein target set used in the study, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Within the 65 target proteins, 56 are predicted intracellular and 9 are predicted secreted.
source: Within the 65 target proteins, 56 are predicted intracellular and 9 are predicted secreted.
evidence: This is a classification of the target proteins based on their predicted localization.

claim: 2.5 log2(TPM +1) was selected as an RNA-level threshold to select a candidate cell line to create a KO.
source: After our initial experience with a few dozen targets comparing RNA expression and the ability to detect a clear signal, we selected 2.5 log2(TPM +1) as an RNA-level threshold to select a candidate cell line to create a KO.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on empirical testing of RNA expression levels and detection ability.

claim: 8 common cell line backgrounds were prioritized because their doubling time is short and they are amenable to CRISPR-Cas9 technology.
source: Among the cell lines showing expression above this level, we prioritized a group of 8 common cell line backgrounds representing different cell/tissue types because their doubling time is short, and they are amenable to CRISPR-Cas9 technology (Figure 1B).
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting specific cell lines for the study.

claim: These 8 cell lines were used in 62 out of the 65 antibody characterization studies.
source: These 8 cell lines were used in 62 out of the 65 antibody characterization studies (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the cell lines used in the study.

claim: An average of 9.5 antibodies per protein target were received from an average of five different antibody manufacturers.
source: We received on average 9.5 antibodies per protein target contributed from an average of five different antibody manufacturers (Figure 1E, F and G).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the antibodies tested in the study.

claim: For 55/65 of the target proteins, one or more antibodies that successfully immunodetected their cognate protein were identified.
source: For 55/65 of the target proteins, we identified one or more antibodies that successfully immunodetected their cognate protein, identifying well-performing antibodies and validating the efficacy of the KO lines.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Western blot testing of antibodies.

claim: For the remaining nine targets, at least one specific, non-selective antibody that detects the cognate protein by WB but also recognizes unrelated proteins was identified.
source: For the remaining nine targets, we identified at least one specific, non-selective antibody that detects the cognate protein by WB, but also recognizes unrelated proteins, that is, non-specific bands not lost in the KO controls.
evidence: This is a result from the Western blot testing showing antibodies with off-target binding.

claim: All 614 antibodies were tested by IP on non-denaturing cell lysates for intracellular proteins or cell media for secreted proteins.
source: All 614 antibodies were tested by IP on non-denaturing cell lysates for intracellular proteins or cell media for secreted proteins, using WB with a successful antibody from the previous step to evaluate the immunocapture (Figure 1F).
evidence: This describes the immunoprecipitation testing methodology applied to all antibodies.

claim: All antibodies against intracellular proteins were tested for IF using a mosaic strategy that imaged parental and KO cells in the same visual field.
source: All antibodies against intracellular proteins were tested for IF using a strategy that imaged a mosaic of parental and KO cells in the same visual field to reduce imaging and analysis biases (Figure 1G).
evidence: This describes the immunofluorescence testing methodology used in the study.

claim: All 65 reports are gathered under the Antibody Characterization through Open Science (YCharOS) community on ZENODO.
source: On ZENODO, all 65 reports are gathered under the Antibody Characterization through Open Science (YCharOS) community: https://ZENODO.org/communities/ycharos/ (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a factual statement about where the data are publicly available.

claim: Each antibody characterization report underwent technical peer review by a group of scientific advisors from academia and industry.
source: Prior to release, each antibody characterization report underwent technical peer review by a group of scientific advisors from academia and industry (Figure 1H).
evidence: This describes the quality control process for the reports.

claim: Approximately 1.6 million antibodies cover approximately 96% of human proteins according to the Antibody Registry.
source: The Antibody Registry (https://www.antibodyregistry.org, RRID:SCR_006397) indicates that there are ~1.6 million antibodies covering ~96% of human proteins (Bandrowski et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bandrowski et al., 2023 and reference to the Antibody Registry database.

claim: 53% of human proteins are covered by at least five renewable antibodies.
source: with 53% covered by at least five renewable antibodies (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Antibody Registry database as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Approximately 21% of human proteins are covered by only one or two renewable antibodies.
source: Approximately 21% of human proteins are covered by only one or two renewable antibodies, and ~15% have no renewable antibodies available (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Antibody Registry database as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Approximately 15% of human proteins have no renewable antibodies available.
source: Approximately 21% of human proteins are covered by only one or two renewable antibodies, and ~15% have no renewable antibodies available (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Antibody Registry database as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the set of 65 proteins, 49 were covered by at least 3 renewable antibodies, 15 by 1 or 2 renewable antibodies, and 1 was not covered by any renewables.
source: In our set of 65 proteins, and from the manufacturers represented, 49 were covered by at least 3 renewable antibodies, 15 by 1 or 2 renewable antibodies, and 1 was not covered by any renewables (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the renewable antibody coverage for the specific protein set tested.

claim: A well-performing renewable antibody was found for 50 targets in WB.
source: We found a well-performing renewable antibody for 50 targets in WB (Figure 2B, left bar graph)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Western blot testing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A well-performing renewable antibody was found for 49 targets in IP.
source: for 49 targets in IP (Figure 2B, middle bar graph)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the immunoprecipitation testing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A well-performing renewable antibody was found for 30 targets in IF.
source: and for 30 targets in IF (Figure 2B, right bar graph)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the immunofluorescence testing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Approximately 40% of the protein set lacked a successful antibody for IF.
source: Some proteins were not covered by any successful antibodies depending on application; notably ~40% of our protein set lacked a successful antibody for IF (Figure 2B, right bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the immunofluorescence testing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The antibody set constituted 258 polyclonal antibodies, 165 monoclonal antibodies and 191 recombinants.
source: The antibody set constituted 258 polyclonal antibodies, 165 monoclonal antibodies and 191 recombinants.
evidence: This is a breakdown of the antibody types tested in the study.

claim: For WB, 27% of the polyclonal antibodies, 41% of the monoclonal antibodies and 67% of the recombinant antibodies immunodetected their target protein.
source: For WB, 27% of the polyclonal antibodies, 41% of the monoclonal antibodies and 67% of the recombinant antibodies immunodetected their target protein (Figure 3, left bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of antibody performance by type in Western blot, shown in Figure 3.

claim: For IP, 39% of polyclonal, 32% of monoclonal and 54% of recombinants successfully immunocaptured their target.
source: For IP, trends were similar: 39%, 32% and 54% of polyclonal, monoclonal and recombinants, respectively (Figure 3, middle bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of antibody performance by type in immunoprecipitation, shown in Figure 3.

claim: For IF, 22% of polyclonal antibodies, 31% of monoclonal antibodies, and 48% of recombinant antibodies generated selective fluorescence signals.
source: For IF, we tested 529 antibodies against the set of intracellular proteins; 22% of polyclonal antibodies, 31% of monoclonal antibodies, and 48% of recombinant antibodies generated selective fluorescence signals in images of parental versus KO cells (Figure 3, right bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of antibody performance by type in immunofluorescence, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Recombinant antibodies are on average better performers than polyclonal or monoclonal antibodies in each of the applications.
source: Thus, recombinant antibodies are on average better performers than polyclonal or monoclonal antibodies in each of the applications.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative performance data across all three applications.

claim: The superior performance of recombinant antibodies could be a consequence of enhanced internal characterization by the commercial suppliers.
source: It should be noted that recombinant antibodies are newer protein reagents compared to polyclonal and monoclonal hybridomas, and their superior performance could be a consequence of enhanced internal characterization by the commercial suppliers.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed superior performance of recombinant antibodies.

claim: Success in IF is the best predictor of performance in WB and IP.
source: However, we find that success in IF is the best predictor of performance in WB and IP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (McNemar test) of correlations between antibody performance across applications, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 578 of the 614 antibodies tested were recommended for WB by the manufacturers.
source: In all, 578 of the 614 antibodies tested were recommended for WB by the manufacturers.
evidence: This is a factual statement about manufacturer recommendations for the tested antibodies.

claim: Of the 578 antibodies recommended for WB, 44% were successful, 35% were specific but non-selective, and 21% failed.
source: Of these, 44% were successful, 35% were specific but non-selective, and 21% failed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, left bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of antibody performance compared to manufacturer recommendations, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Of 614 antibodies, 143 were recommended for IP by the suppliers, and 58% enriched their cognate target from cell extracts.
source: Of 614 antibodies, 143 were recommended for IP, and 58% enriched their cognate target from cell extracts.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of antibody performance in IP compared to manufacturer recommendations.

claim: Of the 471 antibodies that had no recommendation for IP, 37% were able to enrich their cognate antigen.
source: Interestingly, of the 471 remaining antibodies that had no recommendation for IP, 37% were able to enrich their cognate antigen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, middle bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing that many antibodies not recommended for IP can actually perform well in this application.

claim: Of the 529 antibodies tested in IF, 293 were recommended for this application by the suppliers and 236 were not.
source: Of the 529 antibodies tested in IF, 293 were recommended for this application by the suppliers and 236 were not.
evidence: This is a factual statement about manufacturer recommendations for IF.

claim: Only 39% of the antibodies recommended for IF were successful.
source: Only 39% of the antibodies recommended for IF were successful (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, right bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of antibody performance in IF compared to manufacturer recommendations.

claim: For WB, 61% of antibodies were recommended by manufacturers based on orthogonal approaches, 30% based on genetic approaches and 9% using other strategies.
source: For WB, 61% of antibodies were recommended by manufacturers based on orthogonal approaches, 30% based on genetic approaches and 9% using other strategies.
evidence: This is an analysis of the validation methods used by manufacturers for WB recommendations.

claim: For IF, 83% of the antibodies were recommended based on orthogonal approaches, 7% using genetic approaches and 10% using other strategies.
source: For IF, 83% of the antibodies were recommended based on orthogonal approaches, 7% using genetic approaches and 10% using other strategies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an analysis of the validation methods used by manufacturers for IF recommendations, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For WB, 80% of the antibodies recommended by the manufacturers based on orthogonal strategies could detect the intended target protein.
source: For WB, 80% of the antibodies recommended by the manufacturers based on orthogonal strategies and 89% of antibodies recommended based on genetic strategies could detect the intended target protein (Figure 4B, left bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of validation method effectiveness for WB, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For WB, 89% of antibodies recommended based on genetic strategies could detect the intended target protein.
source: For WB, 80% of the antibodies recommended by the manufacturers based on orthogonal strategies and 89% of antibodies recommended based on genetic strategies could detect the intended target protein (Figure 4B, left bar graph).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of validation method effectiveness for WB, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For IF, 38% of the antibodies recommended by the manufacturers based on orthogonal strategies were confirmed using KO cells as controls.
source: For IF, 38% of the antibodies recommended by the manufacturers based on orthogonal strategies were confirmed using KO cells as controls.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of validation method effectiveness for IF.

claim: Of the 20 antibodies validated by the manufacturers for IF on the basis of genetic strategies, 16 (80%) were confirmed in this study.
source: Of the 20 antibodies validated by the manufacturers for IF on the basis of genetic strategies, we confirmed the performance of 16 (80%) (Figure 4B, histogram right).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of validation method effectiveness for IF, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Genetic strategies generate far more robust characterization data for IF than orthogonal strategies.
source: Thus, while orthogonal strategies are somewhat suitable for WB, genetic strategies generate far more robust characterization data for IF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effectiveness of different validation methods across applications.

claim: From a total of 409 antibodies that presented conflicting data between the characterization data and antibody supplier's recommendations, the participating companies have withdrawn 73 antibodies from the market and changed recommendations for 153 antibodies.
source: From a total of 409 antibodies that presented conflicting data between our characterization data and antibody supplier's recommendations, the participating companies have withdrawn 73 antibodies from the market and changed recommendations for 153 antibodies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of actions taken by manufacturers in response to the characterization data, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 2010 publications employed one of the 180 antibodies tested for WB.
source: We identified 2010 publications that employed one of the 180 antibodies we tested for WB.
evidence: This is based on bibliometric analysis using CiteAb to track antibody usage in the literature.

claim: Of the 2010 publications using tested WB antibodies, 69% used a well-performing antibody while 31% used an antibody unsuccessful in the study protocol.
source: Of those, 69% used a well-performing antibody that specifically immunodetected its target protein by WB, while 31% used an antibody unsuccessful in our protocol (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the literature impact of underperforming antibodies, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 105 publications employed 41 of the tested antibodies for IP, with 65% using a well-performing antibody but 35% employing an antibody unable to immunocapture its target protein.
source: For IP, 105 publications employed 41 of our tested antibodies while 65% of these used a well-performing antibody but 35% employed an antibody unable to immunocapture its target protein (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the literature impact of underperforming antibodies for IP, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 548 publications employed 80 of the antibodies tested for IF, with 22% using an antibody unable to immunolocalize its target protein.
source: For IF, we found 548 publications that employed 80 of the antibodies we tested. Of these publications, 22% used an antibody unable to immunolocalize its target protein (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the literature impact of underperforming antibodies for IF, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 88% of publications using unsuccessful IF antibodies contained no validation data.
source: with 88% containing no validation data (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of validation practices in publications using unsuccessful IF antibodies, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: If the results are representative, 20-30% of figures in the literature are generated using antibodies that do not recognize their intended target.
source: If our results are representative, this suggests that 20–30% of figures in the literature are generated using antibodies that do not recognize their intended target, and that more effort in antibody characterization is highly justified.
evidence: This is an extrapolation from the bibliometric data to estimate the broader impact on the literature.

claim: Antibody characterization data generated by this organization are being disseminated through the RRID community and are directly connected through the Antibody Registry, the RRID Portal and participating antibody manufacturers' websites.
source: Antibody characterization data generated by this organization are being disseminated by the RRID community and are directly connected through the Antibody Registry, or the RRID Portal (Figure 5, bottom left image) and participating antibody manufacturers' websites (Figure 5, top image).
evidence: This describes the data dissemination strategy, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The process robustly identifies antibodies that fail to recognize their intended target.
source: Nevertheless, the process robustly identifies antibodies that fail to recognize their intended target, which becomes evident when other antibodies tested in parallel perform well.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the effectiveness of the validation approach based on the comparative testing strategy.

claim: At a minimum, removal of poorly performing products from the market will have significant impact in that hundreds of published papers report the use of such antibodies.
source: At a minimum, removal of these poorly performing products from the market will have significant impact in that hundreds of published papers report the use of such antibodies.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential impact of removing underperforming antibodies, based on the bibliometric data.

claim: In the set of 65 proteins, an average of approximately 12 papers per protein included use of an antibody that failed to recognize the intended protein target using the study protocols.
source: In our set of 65 proteins, we found that an average of ~12 papers per protein included use of an antibody that failed to recognize the intended protein target using our protocols.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the bibliometric analysis showing the extent of underperforming antibody usage in the literature.

claim: The cost of characterizing antibodies for a single protein is estimated at approximately $25,000 USD.
source: In addition, even with our optimized protocol, the cost of characterizing antibodies for a single protein is estimated at ~$25,000 USD.
evidence: This is a cost estimate based on the authors' experience with the validation process.

claim: The cost to characterize antibodies against all proteins in a proteome is estimated at $50 million USD, considering parallelization and industrialization of the procedure.
source: We estimate a cost of $50 million USD to characterize antibodies against all proteins in a proteome, considering parallelization and industrialization of the procedure.
evidence: This is a cost estimate extrapolated from the per-protein cost to the entire proteome.

claim: The estimated cost for validation is far below the predicted waste on bad antibodies, currently estimated at approximately $1B/year.
source: However, it should be noted that this estimated cost for validation is far below the predicted waste on bad antibodies, currently estimated at ~$1B/year (Voskuil et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison of the estimated validation cost to the estimated waste from bad antibodies, with citation to Voskuil et al., 2020.

claim: Independent antibody characterization with openly published data, funded by various global organizations, is certain to save large amounts of money and increase the quality and reproducibility of the literature.
source: Thus, independent antibody characterization with openly published data, funded by various global organizations, is an important, if not essential, initiative that is certain to save large amounts of money and increase the quality and reproducibility of the literature.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the value of the validation initiative based on the cost-benefit analysis.

claim: 15 proteins (23% of the protein sample) are well studied with more than 500 publications.
source: a search of the NIH protein database revealed that 15 proteins (23% of our protein sample) are well studied with more than 500 publications
evidence: This is based on a search of the NIH protein database to assess the level of study for each protein.

claim: 50 proteins (77% of the protein sample) have corresponding publications ranging from 37 to 498.
source: and 50 proteins (77% of our protein sample) have corresponding publications ranging from 37 to 498 (Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is based on a search of the NIH protein database to assess the level of study for each protein.

claim: There are more commercial antibodies available for the best-studied proteins.
source: Although we observed that there are more commercial antibodies available for the best-studied proteins (Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the number of available antibodies to the publication count for each protein.

claim: More than half of the protein targets are covered by well-performing, renewable antibodies for WB, IP and IF - including both well characterized and more poorly studied proteins.
source: an encouraging result of our work is that more than half of our protein targets are covered by well-performing, renewable antibodies for WB, IP and IF - including both well characterized and more poorly studied proteins
evidence: This is a summary finding from the antibody testing across the protein set.

claim: A successful renewable antibody for WB was found for 77% of proteins (50/65).
source: Within the antibodies we tested, we found a successful renewable antibody for WB for 77% of proteins (50/65)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Western blot testing.

claim: A successful renewable antibody for IP was found for 75% of proteins (49/65).
source: for IP for 75% of proteins (49/65)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the immunoprecipitation testing.

claim: A successful renewable antibody for IF was found for 54% of proteins (30/56) examined.
source: and for IF for 54% of proteins (30/56) examined
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the immunofluorescence testing.

claim: It might be possible to identify well-performing renewable reagents for half the human proteome by mining commercial collections.
source: Extrapolation of our findings to the human proteome would suggest that it might be possible to identify well-performing renewable reagents for half the human proteome, including poorly characterized proteins, simply by mining commercial collections.
evidence: This is an extrapolation from the study results to the entire human proteome.

claim: The coverage is likely greater because the corporate partners only represent 27% of the antibody production worldwide.
source: Indeed, it is likely that the coverage is greater because our corporate partners only represent 27% of the antibody production worldwide.
evidence: This is an inference that the actual coverage may be higher based on the limited representation of manufacturers in the study.

claim: Polyclonal antibodies suffer from batch-to-batch variation and are thus in conflict with the scientific community desire to use and provide only renewable reagents.
source: From a scientific perspective, polyclonal antibodies suffer from batch-to-batch variation and are thus in conflict with the scientific community desire to use and provide only renewable reagents.
evidence: This is a statement about a known limitation of polyclonal antibodies based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The generation of polyclonal antibodies requires large numbers of animals yearly.
source: From an ethical perspective, the generation of polyclonal antibodies requires large numbers of animals yearly (Gray et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gray et al., 2016.

claim: Recombinant antibodies may rely on the use of animals for the initiation of an antibody generation program, but animal-free in vitro molecular strategies are also used for production.
source: While recombinant antibodies may rely on the use of animals for the initiation of an antibody generation program, animal-free in vitro molecular strategies are also used for production, and to generate new batches of these antibodies (Gray et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gray et al., 2020.

claim: The uptake of recombinant antibodies by the scientific community has not been satisfactory.
source: As of today, the uptake of recombinant antibodies by the scientific community has not been satisfactory.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of recombinant antibody adoption in the scientific community.

claim: Leading antibody manufacturers are converting top-cited polyclonal antibodies into recombinant antibodies and removing underperforming antibodies from their catalogues.
source: For example, while leading antibody manufacturers are converting top-cited polyclonal antibodies into recombinant antibodies and removing underperforming antibodies from their catalogues, polyclonals remain the most purchased.
evidence: This is a statement about current industry practices in antibody manufacturing.

claim: Polyclonals remain the most purchased antibodies despite manufacturers' efforts to promote recombinant antibodies.
source: For example, while leading antibody manufacturers are converting top-cited polyclonal antibodies into recombinant antibodies and removing underperforming antibodies from their catalogues, polyclonals remain the most purchased.
evidence: This is a statement about current market trends in antibody purchasing.

claim: A lack of understanding in the use of recombinant methods has been suggested by authors of a recent correspondence to the editors of Nature Biotechnology.
source: This situation has also been acknowledged by the EU Reference Laboratory for Alternatives to Animal Testing and a lack of understanding in the use of recombinant methods has been suggested by authors of a recent correspondence to the editors of Nature Biotechnology (Gray et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gray et al., 2020.

claim: One reason for confusion about recombinant antibodies could be the absence of large-scale performance data comparing the various antibody generation technologies.
source: One reason for this confusion could be the absence of large-scale performance data comparing the various antibody generation technologies.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of recombinant antibody adoption.

claim: Recombinant antibodies performed well in all applications tested, arguing there is no reason not to adopt the recombinant technology.
source: In our dataset, recombinant antibodies performed well in all applications tested, arguing there is no reason not to adopt the recombinant technology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative performance data of recombinant antibodies.

claim: Future antibody generation programs should focus on recombinant technologies.
source: Moreover, our study strongly supports the idea that future antibody generation programs should focus on recombinant technologies.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the superior performance of recombinant antibodies in the study.

claim: Using KO (or knockdown in the case of an essential gene) strategies to screen antibodies for the intended application will provide the most effective approach to identify selective antibodies.
source: Given that it is difficult to imagine a characterization pipeline dependent on IF, we suggest that using KO (or knockdown in the case of an essential gene) strategies to screen antibodies for the intended application will provide the most effective approach to identify selective antibodies.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis of validation method effectiveness.

claim: One of the main barriers to large-scale production of high-quality antibodies is the lack of availability of KO lines derived from cells that express detectable levels of each human protein.
source: Currently, one of the main barriers to large-scale production of high-quality antibodies is the lack of availability of KO lines derived from cells that express detectable levels of each human protein.
evidence: This is an assessment of a key limitation in scaling antibody validation efforts.

claim: Creation of a broadly accessible biobank of bespoke KO cells for each human gene should be a priority for the community.
source: Creation of a broadly accessible biobank of bespoke KO cells for each human gene should be a priority for the community.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future infrastructure development to support antibody validation.

claim: The project provides the global life sciences community with a tremendous resource for the study of human proteins and will result in significant improvements in rigour and reproducibility in antibody-based assays and scientific discovery.
source: Overall, this project provides the global life sciences community with a tremendous resource for the study of human proteins and will result in significant improvements in rigour and reproducibility in antibody-based assays and scientific discovery.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the expected impact of the project.

claim: A successful primary antibody for Western blot immunodetects the target protein, and the signal observed in the WT lysate is lost in the KO lysates, and does not recognize other proteins under the conditions tested.
